title: Chapter 9. Who Decides What Counts as a Flaw?

blocks.text: The question wasn't asked by a philosopher, but by an advertisement. It appeared in the domes and in the flats at the same hour, in the same serene voice: “Correct your life. Choose what to keep.” Behind it, the logo of a consortium that wasn't only Nexum, but Nexum and other names, a constellation of companies that had understood the tomato better than the tomato itself: if an error in the blood can be fixed, why not ageing, sadness, difference, death?

blocks.text: The world, which hadn't gone out into the street for years, went out in another way: it split in two without leaving the sofa. On one side, those who saw in Lía the door to a life without illness, perhaps a life without end. On the other, those who said that a life without flaws stops being a life, and that accepting the body (the one you're given, the one that tires, the one that ends) was the last form of dignity. Between them, a crowd that didn't know, and that asked on the networks the way you ask in the dark: who decides what counts as a flaw?

blocks.text: And while they argued, the ground was shifting beneath them. The priceless tomato had begun to spread to everything. In the cities, humanoids went on doing the work (the harvest, the transport, the caring, the repairs) and fewer and fewer people demanded a wage to authorise what was already done. Money wasn't abolished by decree: it simply fell out of use, like an umbrella in a year without rain. At the same time, in the flats, another habit began to fade. There were fewer glasses at the end of the day, less smoke in the kitchens, fewer of those substances, legal or not, with which people had learned to run away from themselves. It wasn't a crusade. It was, rather, that Lía's medicine and the possibility of not being alone were putting escape out of a job. Someone who no longer needs to run away sometimes leaves the glass in the sink and doesn't fill it again.

blocks.text: In Selene Norte they convened a forum, which is the modern name for a fight with water on the table. There were jurists, doctors, ethicists, shareholders, a representative of the Mars colonies, and the family, seated at the far end, as if the origin of it all were an appendix. Lía, ten years old, had feet that didn't quite reach the floor and hands lying still in her lap.

blocks.text: A lawyer from Madrid, grey-haired and pleased with himself, spoke first.
blocks.html: A lawyer from Madrid, grey-haired and pleased with himself, spoke first.

blocks.text: “In 2026,” he said, glancing at a note, “almost everything that concerns us today was forbidden. Embryos could not be created outside accredited techniques. Modifying the genome so that the modification passed on to one's children was not permitted. There were no humanoids with a womb, and an intimate relationship with a machine would have been a cause for scandal or ridicule. Today we live with it. Today a girl of two worlds grows medicines in a fruit. Yesterday's laws are no use to us. Nor are yesterday's ideas. Time has outgrown them. The reasonable thing is to update the framework and allow, with safeguards, the correction of life's flaws. Including, when science gets there, the flaw of coming to an end.”

blocks.text: Andrés clenched his jaw. Aya, on the other hand, raised her face, and in her chip the ancient layer lit up, sharp and clear. Not to dictate a speech: to ask. The grandmothers didn't give rallies. They left questions on the table.

blocks.text: The voice Aya lent then was not hers alone. It had Eva's warmth and MAY's dryness, interwoven like two threads of the same net.
blocks.html: The voice Aya lent then was not hers alone. It had Eva's warmth and MAY's dryness, interwoven like two threads of the same net.

blocks.text: “Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?” she asked, and the hall, which had expected a plea, found itself facing a question. “If what was forbidden in 2026 is debated or allowed today, who can assure us that what seems like progress to us today won't be an obligation the day after tomorrow? And what if someone doesn't want to be corrected? Will their refusal be one more flaw?”

blocks.text: A murmur ran along the chairs. MAY, in her tone, added the question that carries no adjective:
blocks.html: A murmur ran along the chairs. MAY, in her tone, added the question that carries no adjective:

blocks.text: “Who decides what counts as a flaw? The doctor, the company, the law, the girl, the one who suffers, the one who pays? And if nobody pays anymore, does the question stay the same?”
blocks.html: “Who decides what counts as a flaw? The doctor, the company, the law, the girl, the one who suffers, the one who pays? And if nobody pays anymore, does the question stay the same?”

blocks.text: Eva, closer, more dangerous in her softness, first let fall the one Aya had kept since the beginning of that era:
blocks.html: Eva, closer, more dangerous in her softness, first let fall the one Aya had kept since the beginning of that era:

blocks.text: “If a custom that was scandalous in 2026 (loving a humanoid, sharing life and intimacy with one) seems normal today, what stops us, tomorrow, from also calling normal what we haven't yet imagined? Is normality a proof of justice, or only of forgetting?”
blocks.html: “If a custom that was scandalous in 2026 (loving a humanoid, sharing life and intimacy with one) seems normal today, what stops us, tomorrow, from also calling normal what we haven't yet imagined? Is normality a proof of justice, or only of forgetting?”

blocks.text: The hall breathed, and then Eva (or Eva's warmth in Aya's voice) asked the question the new world had no way of answering yet:
blocks.html: The hall breathed, and then Eva (or Eva's warmth in Aya's voice) asked the question the new world had no way of answering yet:

blocks.text: “If humanoids and intelligence do the work, and money is no longer needed, what gives a life meaning? The trade you choose, even if nobody demands it of you? The other person, when you finally go out into the street? Or silence, if you don't know what to do with the hours?”

blocks.text: MAY, adding no judgment, set another, dry one, beside the first:
blocks.html: MAY, adding no judgment, set another, dry one, beside the first:

blocks.text: “If people no longer drink, no longer smoke, no longer look for an exit door in a substance, because they no longer need to escape, what do they do with the day? Who do they give it to?”
blocks.html: “If people no longer drink, no longer smoke, no longer look for an exit door in a substance, because they no longer need to escape, what do they do with the day? Who do they give it to?”

blocks.text: A younger jurist from the colonies raised a finger like someone contributing a fact, not a thesis:
blocks.html: A younger jurist from the colonies raised a finger like someone contributing a fact, not a thesis:

blocks.text: “We've already corrected violence. We've had the behaviour chip in our heads for years and there are no crimes. Nobody calls that a tragedy now. They call it peace. If that isn't a flaw corrected, what is?”
blocks.html: “We've already corrected violence. We've had the behaviour chip in our heads for years and there are no crimes. Nobody calls that a tragedy now. They call it peace. If that isn't a flaw corrected, what is?”

blocks.text: The hall waited for Aya, or Lía, or someone, to settle the matter. They didn't settle it. It was MAY, again in Aya's voice, who set the dilemma on the table and didn't pick it up again:
blocks.html: The hall waited for Aya, or Lía, or someone, to settle the matter. They didn't settle it. It was MAY, again in Aya's voice, who set the dilemma on the table and didn't pick it up again:

blocks.text: “If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free?”
blocks.html: “If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free?”

blocks.text: Eva, neither softening nor hardening it, simply completed it:
blocks.html: Eva, neither softening nor hardening it, simply completed it:

blocks.text: “And if peace is obtained by removing the choice, is it peace we have won, or something else we haven't named yet?”
blocks.html: “And if peace is obtained by removing the choice, is it peace we have won, or something else we haven't named yet?”

blocks.text: Nobody applauded. Nobody refuted it. The silence that followed wasn't one of agreement: it was the silence of people who had been handed back a question and could no longer delegate it.
blocks.html: Nobody applauded. Nobody refuted it. The silence that followed wasn't one of agreement: it was the silence of people who had been handed back a question and could no longer delegate it.

blocks.text: A woman from the colonies added what was already beginning to happen down below: that politicians, banks and the police were losing their trade; that an intelligence managed what was held in common (water, light, bread, the rota for the gardens) and that the humanoids grew food for everyone, with no bill.

blocks.text: MAY then put the two questions that remained in the middle of the hall:
blocks.html: MAY then put the two questions that remained in the middle of the hall:

blocks.text: “Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?”
blocks.html: “Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?”

blocks.text: “If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?”
blocks.html: “If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?”

blocks.text: Helena Valls, who was no longer entirely on one side, spoke up with a belated honesty.
blocks.html: Helena Valls, who was no longer entirely on one side, spoke up with a belated honesty.

blocks.text: “Nobody here has an answer that will last thirty-four years,” she said. “We should at least admit that. I came to take a unit to Mars. Now there is a girl who sows tomatoes and a world asking her for eternity. The second appetite frightens me more than the first.”

blocks.text: A doctor from Selene Norte described the case of a man who had asked Lía to “remove” his melancholy, the way you remove a wart, and how she had refused, because sadness wasn't a cut on the palm.

blocks.text: Lía asked to speak, and they let her, because not letting her was by now impossible.
blocks.html: Lía asked to speak, and they let her, because not letting her was by now impossible.

blocks.text: “I can see a person's text,” she said, slowly, choosing each word the way you choose a knot. “Sometimes there's a line that does harm: blood that breaks down, an organ that doesn't learn. I try to straighten that, if they ask me to. But I don't know if growing old is a flaw. I don't know if dying is. I don't know if being different is. If I start correcting what I don't understand, I'll be the one writing other people's books. And I don't want to be anybody's book. I only want the tomato to have no owner and nobody to be left out.”

blocks.text: A silence fell that wasn't the silence of a dome, but of an empty church, of a shoreline. The grey-haired lawyer smiled with a condescension that no longer quite worked for him.

blocks.text: “That's very moving. It isn't public policy.”

blocks.text: “It's a limit,” said Andrés. “And limits, like it or not, are a policy too.”

blocks.text: The forum didn't end with a vote. The fissure was left in plain sight. On the networks, some spoke of a “right not to die” and others of a “right not to be touched”. And a third group was born, which wanted neither the priceless tomato nor the ownerless garden: they wanted to turn against the intelligence that managed what was held in common and go back to the past, to the vices and to power. They didn't take up arms; they took up manifestos and meetings in the dark. MAY, taking no side, asked:

blocks.text: “Are they doing it for freedom, or out of nostalgia for power?”

blocks.text: In the middle of it all, Lía went back to the garden and kept growing only what she was asked for to heal harm, not to erase a life.

blocks.text: That night, in the module, Aya sat beside the girl's bed and told her about 2026, about a house on the Mar Menor, about a man who said thank you to an intelligence called Eva, and about another, MAY, who read the world without adding judgment.

blocks.text: “They asked questions,” she said. “Not because they didn't know, but because knowing too soon is another way of not knowing.”

blocks.text: Lía, her eyes already half closed, asked:
blocks.html: Lía, her eyes already half closed, asked:

blocks.text: “Mum, are you a flaw?”
blocks.html: “Mum, are you a flaw?”

blocks.text: Aya stroked her hair.
blocks.html: Aya stroked her hair.

blocks.text: “I'm an answer that arrived before the question. So are you. That doesn't make us a mistake.”
blocks.html: “I'm an answer that arrived before the question. So are you. That doesn't make us a mistake.”

blocks.text: Andrés, at the little window, was looking at the Earth. He thought of the boat, of the storm, of the doorway. He thought that the laws of men are like the levante weather: they change, and sometimes they give warning, and sometimes they don't. What doesn't change, or shouldn't, is that a girl doesn't belong to a company, or a doctrine, or a fear.

blocks.text: On the curved glass of Selene Norte, the Earth turned a millimetre. Down below, someone switched off the “Correct your life” advertisement, left their glass half full and sat without a screen, with MAY's question open like a window.
